definition: Lasting for a very short time; transitory.
example: The ephemeral beauty of cherry blossoms makes them all the more precious.

etymology.note: From epi (on) + hēmera (day). Originally used in medicine to describe fevers lasting exactly one day.

idiom.meaning: Something that doesn't last or can't be relied upon.

definition: The realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as one's own.
example: A wave of sonder washed over her as she watched strangers cross the rain-soaked street.

etymology.note: To probe or plumb the depths. Coined as a neologism by The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows.

idiom.phrase: walk a mile in someone's shoes
idiom.meaning: To try to understand another person's experience or perspective.

definition: Relating to a transitional stage; occupying a position at or on both sides of a boundary.
example: The hotel corridor at 3am has a distinctly liminal quality — neither night nor day.

etymology.note: Meaning threshold. Used in anthropology to describe the in-between phase of a rite of passage.

idiom.phrase: between a rock and a hard place
idiom.meaning: Caught in a difficult position with no easy way out.

definition: The pleasant, earthy scent produced when rain falls on dry earth.
example: After months of drought, the petrichor from the first storm was almost overwhelming.

etymology.note: Petra (stone) + ichor (the fluid in the veins of the gods). Coined in 1964 by scientists Isabel Bear and R.G. Thomas.

idiom.meaning: To slow down and appreciate the simple pleasures of everyday life.

definition: The strange wistfulness of used bookshops, stemming from their shelves full of books you'll never have time to read.
example: She spent an hour in vellichor, running her fingers over spines she would never open.

etymology.note: Vellum (parchment) + ichor (ethereal fluid). From The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, capturing a specifically literary melancholy.

idiom.phrase: so many books, so little time
idiom.meaning: The feeling that there is more to read or experience than time will ever allow.

definition: Expressed clearly and easy to understand; also, showing the ability to think clearly.
example: Despite his fever, he remained lucid enough to give precise instructions.

etymology.note: From lux (light). Originally meaning bright or shining, later extended to clarity of thought and expression.

idiom.meaning: Completely obvious and easy to understand.

definition: The quality of being open and honest in expression; frankness.
example: She appreciated his candor even when his feedback was difficult to hear.

etymology.note: From candidus (white, pure). Related to candidate — Roman candidates wore white togas as a symbol of purity.

idiom.meaning: Said or done in a direct, honest way without holding back.

definition: Mental calmness and composure, especially in difficult situations.
example: She faced the diagnosis with remarkable equanimity, focusing on what she could control.

etymology.note: From aequus (equal) + animus (mind). A key virtue in Stoic philosophy.

idiom.meaning: To remain calm and think clearly in a stressful situation.

definition: Understood or implied without being stated directly.
example: There was a tacit agreement among the team to never discuss what had happened.

etymology.note: From tacere (to be silent). Related to taciturn — a person who says very little.

idiom.meaning: Something so obvious it doesn't need to be stated.

definition: Translucently clear; easily understood.
example: His pellucid prose made even the most complex ideas feel effortless to grasp.

etymology.note: From per (through) + lucere (to shine). Literally, shining through.

idiom.meaning: To understand the true nature of something, or to complete something to the end.

definition: Too great or extreme to be expressed in words.
example: Standing at the canyon's edge, she felt an ineffable sense of awe.

etymology.note: From in- (not) + effari (to speak out). Originally used in religious contexts for things too sacred to name.

idiom.meaning: So extreme or moving that language cannot adequately describe it.

definition: Optimistic, especially in a difficult situation.
example: Despite the setbacks, he remained sanguine about the project's chances.

etymology.note: From sanguis (blood). In medieval humour theory, a sanguine temperament — associated with blood — was linked to cheerfulness.

idiom.meaning: To be optimistic and focus on the positive aspects of a situation.

definition: Showing a casual lack of concern; carefree.
example: He strolled into the meeting late with an insouciant smile, as if time were an abstraction.

etymology.note: From in- (not) + soucier (to worry). Entered English in the 19th century, retaining its French flavor.

idiom.meaning: To be completely indifferent to something.

definition: Full of danger or uncertainty; perilous.
example: The company found itself in a parlous state after the market collapsed.

etymology.note: A contraction of perilous, from Old French perillous. Fell out of common use but persists in literary and formal English.

idiom.meaning: In a risky or precarious situation.

definition: Excessive pride or self-confidence, often leading to downfall.
example: His hubris in dismissing all feedback ultimately led to the product's failure.

etymology.note: In Greek tragedy, hubris was the fatal flaw — overreaching defiance of the gods that always preceded nemesis.

idiom.meaning: Behaving as if one is more important or capable than one actually is.

definition: A pleasant feeling of tiredness or lack of energy; dreamy inactivity.
example: The long afternoon heat induced a languor that made work feel impossible.

etymology.note: From languere (to be faint or weak). Related to languid and languish.

idiom.meaning: To relax and not exert oneself.

definition: The appearance of being true or real.
example: The novel's meticulous period detail gave it a verisimilitude that made readers forget it was fiction.

etymology.note: From verus (true) + similis (like). Literally, likeness to truth.

idiom.meaning: To seem genuine or believable.

definition: Using very few words; brief and concise.
example: His laconic reply — just two words — somehow said everything.

etymology.note: From Lakonia, the region of Sparta, whose inhabitants were famous for terse speech. When Philip of Macedon threatened invasion, Spartans replied with a single word: 'If.'

idiom.meaning: Someone who does not talk much, often implying quiet strength.

definition: Tending to disappear; fleeting.
example: Youth is fugacious — it slips away before you realize you had it.

etymology.note: From fugere (to flee). Related to fugitive and refuge.

idiom.meaning: To lose something valuable before you can hold on to it.

definition: Expressing a particular point of view; promoting a cause.
example: The report was criticized for being tendentious rather than objective.

etymology.note: From tendere (to stretch or aim toward). Carries a slightly negative connotation of bias.

idiom.meaning: To have a personal motive behind an argument or action.

definition: Sweet or musical; pleasant to hear.
example: Her mellifluous voice made even a routine announcement feel like a performance.

etymology.note: From mel (honey) + fluere (to flow). Literally, flowing with honey.

idiom.meaning: Something very pleasing to hear.

definition: Clear, logical, and convincing.
example: She made a cogent argument for restructuring the process.

etymology.note: From co- (together) + agere (to drive). To drive together, to compel.

idiom.meaning: To argue persuasively in support of something.

definition: Light, delicate, and thin; insubstantial.
example: The fog rolled in like gossamer curtains, softening every edge of the harbor.

etymology.note: Originally referred to fine spider webs seen in autumn fields, possibly from the time of year when geese were eaten. The delicate threads became a metaphor for anything filmy and light.

idiom.meaning: Almost insubstantial; barely there.

definition: Self-confidence and assurance, especially in demanding situations.
example: She handled the unexpected questions with total aplomb.

etymology.note: From à plomb (according to the plumb line). Straight and true — the confidence that comes from being perfectly balanced.

idiom.meaning: To remain calm under pressure.

definition: Eternal and unchanging; everlasting.
example: The monastery seemed to exist outside time, caught in a sempiternal quiet.

etymology.note: From semper (always) + aeternus (eternal). Often used in theological contexts.

idiom.meaning: Forever; for as long as anything exists.

definition: Having a ready insight into things; shrewd.
example: A perspicacious observer would have noticed the tension long before it surfaced.

etymology.note: From perspicere (to see through clearly). Related to perspicuous — clear and easy to understand.

idiom.meaning: To understand the hidden meaning behind what is said or written.

definition: A state of physical or mental inactivity; lethargy.
example: After the holiday, he slid into a torpor that lasted well into January.

etymology.note: From torpere (to be numb). Used in biology to describe dormancy in animals.

idiom.meaning: To do something without genuine effort or engagement.

definition: Lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm; going from one thing to another.
example: They made desultory conversation while waiting for the meeting to start.

etymology.note: From desultor — a circus rider who leapt between horses. Jumping around without direction.

idiom.meaning: Disorganized or lacking a clear direction.

definition: Not likely to offend or upset anyone; deliberately inoffensive.
example: The statement was so anodyne it could have been written by a committee of no one.

etymology.note: From an- (without) + odyne (pain). Originally a medical term for a pain-relieving drug.

idiom.meaning: To avoid risks by taking the most cautious option.

definition: The partially shaded outer region of a shadow; the fringes of something.
example: The policy existed in the penumbra of legality — not clearly permitted, not clearly prohibited.

etymology.note: From paene (almost) + umbra (shadow). Used in astronomy to describe the partial shadow during an eclipse.

idiom.meaning: Operating in a hidden or ambiguous area, away from clear scrutiny.
